text: Underwater archaeology applies the methods and ethics of terrestrial archaeology to areas under seas, lakes and rivers. Because submerged environments can preserve organic materials that would disintegrate ashore, shipwrecks and drowned settlements often provide exceptionally rich evidence of past societies. However, it requires special techniques and technologies that can be grouped as follows. **Place and Remote Sensing** Most projects start looking for a website. Researchers combine archive research, historical maps and reports from fishermen and divers with geophysical investigations: - **Side-scan sonar** produces detailed acoustic images of the sea floor that reveal wreck hills, rubble fields and other anomalies. - **Multibeam echosounders** generate high-resolution badymetric maps that show the shape of a wreck and its relationship to the surrounding sea floor. - **Sub-bottom Profiler** penetrate sediment to detect buried structures. - **Seemagnetometer** detect disturbances in the earth's magnetic field caused by iron objects such as anchors, cannons and fortifications. In shallow coastal waters, airborne LiDAR Bathymetry can also be used to map drowned landscapes and coastal wrecks. **Robotic and remote controlled systems** When depth or dangerous conditions exceed the limits of human divers, remote controlled vehicles (ROVs) and autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) are used. ROVs bound to a surface vessel carry cameras, lighting, arms of sonar and manipulator and allow archaeologists to inspect, sample and recover objects in real time. AUVs follow preprogrammed survey paths and can map extensive areas with considerable precision. Such systems have made it possible to study deep waters, including well-preserved old wrecks identified in the oxygen-free depths of the Black Sea. ==References====External links== For locations within the reach of divers, specialized equipment extends both safe working hours and operational depth. Open-Circuit SCUBA remains standard in shallow water, while surface air, mixed gas techniques and closed-circuit rebreathers allow longer and deeper dives. Saturation diving allows the staff to work with a single decompression at the end of the procedure into depth for longer periods of time, and atmospheric diving suits that hold the internal pressure in an atmosphere were used in places such as the Antikythera wreck. **Excavation and documentation** The underwater excavation follows the same strict principles as the work on land. A grid or baseline is defined so that each find can be located within a three-dimensional frame and fine sediments are removed with hand vents, air lifts or water strokes that are overloaded without damaging fragile material. Acoustic positioning systems, together with traditional offset measurements, capture the exact position of artifacts and structural elements. The documentation was transformed by digital methods. Photogrammetry, in which overlapping photographs are processed into precise three-dimensional models, makes it possible to record a location in detail, to measure it at a later stage and to share it with scientists and the public through virtual reconstructions. Laser and structured light scanning serve a similar purpose for individual artifacts. **Maintenance and scientific analysis** Items that have been under water for centuries are chemically and physically unstable as soon as they recover and require immediate preservation. Waterproof wood must be kept moist and impregnated with consolidants such as polyethylene glycol before drying under controlled conditions, as was the case with the Vasa and Mary Rose shells; smaller objects are often freeze-dried. Ceramics and metals require desalination to remove soluble salts, and iron objects enclosed in marine concretion are often examined by X-radiography or computer tomography before cleaning begins. text: The vault door was still swinging when the first bullet hit Daniel Whitmore in the chest. He didn't intend to be shot. In truth, he had not intended to rob a bank, at least three weeks ago, when the foreclosure notice arrived and the last of his savings disappeared into a medical bill. The plan was simple: a mask, a duffel bag, a toy gun he bought from second hand, and ten minutes of courage. The guard, a heavyweight man named Ortiz, fired twice more. Daniel felt every impact as a hard thrust, as if someone pushed him into an overcrowded corridor. He stumbled against a marble column. Then he looked down. There were three holes in his jacket. There was no blood. "Stay down!" cried Ortiz, his voice cracked. He fired again. The round smoothed against Daniel's shoulder and fell to the ground with a small metallic sound. For a moment, the entire lobby remained silent. The plates, the customers lying on the tile, the guard with his smoke gun: all stared at Daniel, and Daniel stared back. "I think," he slowly said, "that something is wrong with the way it works." Ortiz lowered his weapon. His hands trembled. "What are you?" "I don't know," Daniel admitted. He removed the mask because it seemed foolish to keep hiding. "I assure you, this is just as surprising to me as it is to you." Sirens approached in the distance. Daniel looked at his position with the calm of a man who had just discovered that the rules had changed. He could run away with the money. He could, probably, go through the police line unharmed. But when he looked at the frightened faces on the floor, the thought of the duffel bag suddenly felt shameful. He put it on the counter, uncensored and empty. "I apologize for the interruption," he said to the next plate, a young woman who clasped her badge. "I wanted to take money. I won't do that." The police had come into force outside. Daniel stepped into the sunlight with his hands up. Officers screamed. The shots rang, one by one, and everyone beat him and fell harmlessly away. He stood patiently until they stopped. "Gentlemen," he said, "I'm ready to be arrested. I'm just asking someone to tell me why I can't get hurt because I'd love to know." A silence has subsided. Then the commanding officer, pale and insecure, slowly lowered his weapon. Daniel realized that being invincible did not solve his problems. The foreclosure was still waiting at home. The medical bill had not shrunk. But something had changed. For the first time in months, he was not afraid, and he suspected that this change would count more than any money in the vault. He stretched out his wrists. "Please," he said. "Let's start."

text: Girard's geometry of interaction (GoI) provides a dynamic, algebraic account of cut elimination in linear logic in which evidence is interpreted as operators and normalization is expressed by performing a feedback loop between them. While the original construction was developed for the multiplicative exponential fragment, its extension to richer systems has proved to be delicate, especially if one wants to maintain a clear connection with the structure of the evidence. In this article, we examine the geometry of interaction for polarized linear logic (LLP), a variant in which formulas are divided into positive and negative classes and structural rules. This discipline makes LLP a natural target language for the translation of call-by-value and call-by-name Lambda Calculi, and so a GoI for it also sheds light on the execution of functional programs. We define an interpretation of LLP proofs as partial isometry on a Hilbert space of token configurations, and we show that the execution formula converges exactly when the proof normalizes. The polarity limitation plays a central role, which allows us to treat the exponential modalities with the help of a simple duplicate mechanism, rather than the complete machinery of boxes and their auxiliary ports. We prove the solidity of the interpretation in terms of cut elimination, and we provide the appropriateness for the polarized fragment by connecting our semantics to a token machine. Finally, we describe how the construction is responsible for a standard continuity-passing translation, and discuss possible connections with game emantics and with the implementation of efficient abstract machines.
